The Halakhic Teaching and Public Work of Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer (Baruch She'amar): A Renaissance of the Craft of STaM in Ashkenaz and the Land of Israel
The article surveys the monumental work of Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer, called "Baruch She'amar," who worked in the 14th century to restore and establish the craft of STaM (Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot) in Ashkenaz and the Land of Israel. The text describes how a young orphan became a supreme halakhic authority whose canonical work, the book "Baruch She'amar," constitutes to this day the main foundation for the laws of writing the letters and their form, known as the **"Beit Yosef script"**. The source emphasizes Rabbi Shimshon's journeys to correct corruptions in the scribal tradition and the unique literary structure of his work, which combines halakha, technical tradition and kabbalistic secrets. Ultimately, the article presents his figure as a historical bridge that ensured the continuity of the sacred tradition and of halakhic precision from generation to generation.
The Halakhic Teaching and Public Work of Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer (Baruch She'amar): A Renaissance of the Craft of STaM in Ashkenaz and the Land of Israel
Historical Introduction: The World of STaM in the Fourteenth Century
The history of the writing of Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot (STaM) underwent significant changes during the fourteenth century, a period in which the Ashkenazi traditions of halakhic ruling took shape in the face of the challenges of the time and of wandering. At the center of this process stands the figure of Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer, called "Baruch She'amar," whose work went beyond mere halakhic instruction and became an enterprise of rescuing ancient scribal traditions and establishing them for later generations.[1, 2] The fourteenth century was characterized by instability for the communities of Ashkenaz, which at times led to neglect of the complex sacred crafts and to the penetration of corruptions into the form of the letters and into the laws of making tefillin.[1, 2] Rabbi Shimshon, who lived and worked in Germany, Prague and the Land of Israel, identified this neglect and devoted his life to remedying the situation, combining deep scholarly knowledge of halakha with supreme technical skill in the scribal craft.[2, 3]
Rabbi Shimshon's importance derives not only from his personality but mainly from the canonical work he left behind – the book "Baruch She'amar." This book is not a single unit but a fabric of knowledge combining the teaching of great Rishonim, among them Rabbi Avraham of Sinzheim (a disciple of the Maharam of Rothenburg), with the glosses and insights of Rabbi Shimshon himself, to which was later added the "Alpha Beta" of his disciple, Rabbi Yom Tov Lipmann Mühlhausen.[1, 4] The influence of this work is so profound that most of the laws of STaM appearing in the "Shulchan Arukh" and known as the "Beit Yosef script" derive directly from the traditions Rabbi Shimshon perpetuated in his writings.[4, 5]
A Biography of Devotion: From Orphanhood to Leadership
Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer was born in the land of Saxony (Sachsen) in Germany at the beginning of the 14th century.[1, 2] In his childhood he moved with his parents to the city of Prague, which was at that time a central Torah crossroads in Europe. When he was only about eight years old, the young Shimshon experienced a severe personal tragedy when he was orphaned of both his parents.[1, 2, 3] This orphanhood did not break his spirit, but led him to find refuge and meaning within the walls of the synagogue and in the care of the sages of the generation.
The Origin of the Name "Baruch She'amar" and Its Family Consequences
The epithet "Baruch She'amar," which accompanied Rabbi Shimshon and over the years became his family name, grew out of a distinctive religious practice he adopted in his childhood.[1, 3] In the introduction to his book he relates that he used to rise early for the synagogue and recite the prayer "Baruch She'amar" ("Blessed is He who spoke") in the pleasant and sweet voice with which the blessed Lord had graced him.[1] The devotion and joy with which he recited the prayer impressed the congregation, until they called him "Shimshon Baruch She'amar."[1, 2, 3] This name did not remain merely a personal epithet; according to the testimony of the Chida in his book "Shem ha-Gedolim," the name became a family inheritance passed down from generation to generation, and references can be found in the "Beit Yosef" to Rabbi Yitzhak Baruch She'amar, who was apparently one of his descendants.[2, 3, 4]
Professional Apprenticeship under Rabbi Yissachar
After he was orphaned, Rabbi Shimshon was adopted by Rabbi Yissachar, who was an expert scribe and a Torah scholar.[2, 3] Rabbi Yissachar recognized the potential latent in the boy and taught him the craft of writing tefillin, mezuzot and Torah scrolls.[2] This apprenticeship was critical, for it not only gave Shimshon a profession but brought him into the chain of transmission of the Ashkenazi scribal craft, which demands precision in technical and halakhic details alike.[2, 3]

Wandering as a Mission of Correction: From Europe to Jerusalem
Rabbi Shimshon did not content himself with staying in one place. He set out on an extensive journey throughout central and eastern Europe, which included Austria, Poland, Lusatia, Thuringia and Bavaria.[2, 3] In every community he came to, he acted as an inspector and instructor for the local scribes of STaM. He discovered great neglect; many scribes did not know the precise halakha, and grave errors had become entrenched in the writing of the letters and in the processing of the parchment.[1, 2] In certain cases his halakhic position was so firm that he instructed certain scribes to stop writing altogether, out of concern that the public would be misled and that invalid sacred objects would come from their hands.[1]
The Encounter with the Scribes of the Land of Israel and the Halakhic Disappointment
The high point of his journeys was his ascent to the Land of Israel.[1, 2] Rabbi Shimshon came to the Land expecting to find there the pure source of the sacred craft, on the assumption that the scribes of the Land preserved the tradition most precisely.[2, 3] However, his hope was disappointed. On arriving in Jerusalem and in other communities in the Land, he discovered that most of the scribes there suffered from deep ignorance regarding the accepted halakha and the traditional form of the letters.[2, 3, 6] This discovery was the main motive for writing his work, since he understood that the need for "correction" was not limited to Ashkenaz alone but was an urgent need of all Jewry. He used his findings in the Land of Israel to establish the need for an orderly halakhic work that would serve as a binding guide for every scribe wherever he might be.[2, 3]
The Literary Structure of the "Baruch She'amar" Collection
The book "Baruch She'amar" as we know it today is in fact a collection bringing together three separate works that merged over the generations into a single halakhic entity.[1, 4] Understanding this structure is essential for assessing the contribution of Rabbi Shimshon, who acted not only as an author but also as an editor and corrector who preserved ancient texts.
1. Tikkun Tefillin by Rabbi Avraham of Sinzheim
The central core of the book is the "Tikkun Tefillin" written by Rabbi Avraham ben Moshe of Sinzheim (around the year 1300).[1, 4, 7] Rabbi Avraham was one of the foremost disciples of the Maharam of Rothenburg, and he represents the peak of Ashkenazi halakha of the 13th century.[1, 4] Rabbi Shimshon testified of him that he was "the head of all the writers of tefillin who were in his generation, and after him none arose like him."[1] The book deals with the technical and practical aspects of making tefillin: processing the hide, making the boxes, scoring the lines for the passages, and the writing itself.[1, 7]
2. The Glosses of Baruch She'amar (Rabbi Shimshon)
Rabbi Shimshon's personal contribution is a series of detailed glosses and notes on the work of Rabbi Avraham.[1, 4] Rabbi Shimshon did not seek to create a new book, but to correct Rabbi Avraham's text, which had been corrupted in the manuscripts, and to add further sources and laws to it.[1, 7] These glosses include rulings from the "Halakhot Gedolot," the Semag (Sefer Mitzvot Gadol), the "Sefer ha-Terumah," the "Sefer ha-Rokeach" and other works.[2, 3] Over time these glosses became an inseparable part of the text, and the name "Baruch She'amar" became the overall name of the combined work.[1]
3. Alpha Beta by Rabbi Yom Tov Lipmann Mühlhausen
The third part of the collection is the book "Alpha Beta" by Rabbi Yom Tov Lipmann Mühlhausen, a dayyan of Prague who lived at the turn of the 14th and 15th centuries.[1, 4] Rabbi Yom Tov was a disciple of Rabbi Shimshon and learned much from him about the scribal craft.[1] His book deals with great precision with the form of the letters, but adds to them a significant layer of reasons according to the Kabbalah and the secrets of the letters.[1, 5] The writing of the "Alpha Beta" lasted thirty-three years, and it gives spiritual and mystical depth to the technical craft described in the previous parts.[1]

The Halakhic Methodology: A Synthesis of Sources and Experience
The teaching of Rabbi Shimshon Baruch She'amar is characterized by a meticulous approach resting on three legs: the tradition of the sages of Ashkenaz, research into the sources of the Geonim, and practical experience in the field. He saw the halakhic text not merely as theoretical instruction but as manufacturer's instructions that must be carried out with almost mathematical precision in order to ensure the holiness of the object.[1, 2, 3]
The Use of Ancient Sources
Rabbi Shimshon was greatly versed in the writings of the Geonim and the early Rishonim. In his glosses he constantly quotes the "Halakhot Gedolot" and the "Shimusha Rabba," an ancient work on the laws of tefillin attributed to the Geonim.[2, 8] He dealt extensively with the description of the "square knot" of the tefillin, relying on ancient versions of Rav Hai Gaon and of Rabbi Yehuda ben Barzilai of Barcelona.[8] His ability to draw information from forgotten sources and make it accessible to scribes turned his book into a kind of encyclopedia of the craft of STaM.
The Struggle over the Form of the Letters and the "Beit Yosef Script"
One of Rabbi Shimshon's most central contributions is the shaping of what is called today the "Beit Yosef script."[4, 5] Although it was Rabbi Yosef Karo who published the laws in section 36 of Orach Chaim, he himself declares that he relies on the book "Baruch She'amar" in all that concerns the custom of Ashkenaz and the form of their letters.[4, 5] Rabbi Shimshon defined with great precision the relations between the parts of the letter, the placement of the crownlets (Tagin), and the laws concerning the "thorn of the yod" according to the view of Rabbenu Tam.[5]
Rabbi Shimshon's precision touched the smallest details:
Sha'atnez Getz (shin, ayin, tet, nun, zayin, gimel, tzadi): insistence on three crownlets above these letters.[5]
Bedek Chayah (bet, dalet, kuf, chet, yod, he): insistence on one crownlet above these letters.[5]
Melakhet Sofer (mem, lamed, alef, kaf, tav, samekh, vav, peh, resh): letters without crownlets, but with specific design requirements.[5]
The Controversy over the "Inverted Tzadi": Between Tradition and Kabbalah
A fascinating question that demonstrates Rabbi Shimshon's lasting influence is the debate over the form of the letter tzadi.[9] According to the description appearing in "Baruch She'amar," the letter tzadi is composed of a bent nun with a yod on it whose head faces right (a straight form). This is the classical Ashkenazi tradition that Rabbi Shimshon perpetuated.[9]
With the spread of the Kabbalah and the writings of the Ari, a custom developed of writing the yod on the back of the tzadi "inverted," that is, facing left. This controversy accompanied the world of STaM for hundreds of years.[9] Whereas the Sephardic tradition and some of the Hasidim adopted the "inverted tzadi," the decisors loyal to the tradition of "Baruch She'amar," headed in recent generations by the "Chazon Ish," insisted that the ancient Ashkenazi tradition brought in the book must not be changed.[9] This debate illustrates how a book written in the 14th century continues to be a firm rock for halakhic discussion in the 20th and 21st centuries as well.
The History of the Printing and Preservation of "Baruch She'amar"
For hundreds of years the book "Baruch She'amar" circulated in manuscripts only.[7] Scribes used to copy it for themselves as part of their professional training. An 18th-century manuscript found recently attests to the level of precision with which the work was preserved, with a clear separation between the original text of Rabbi Avraham and the glosses of Rabbi Shimshon.[7]
The transition to print was not free of difficulties:
The Shklov edition (1804): regarded as one of the central editions, but it suffers from editing and printing corruptions.[2, 3] This edition also included the "Otiyot de-Rabbi Akiva" and further kabbalistic passages that had been added to the book over time.[2, 3]
The Warsaw edition (1877): the Reizman edition, which provided a more accessible text and served students of STaM in Europe at the end of the 19th century.[4]
The fact that the book was printed again and again in the Torah centers of eastern Europe attests that it never lost its importance as a foundational book.[4, 7]
Influence on Later Generations and Its Place in the Jewish Bookcase
The legacy of Rabbi Shimshon Baruch She'amar is not confined to the bookshelf of the scribes of STaM. It forms a bridge between the period of the Rishonim and the period of the Acharonim and a source of authority for everyone who deals with the laws of writing and holiness.
The Influence on Later Halakhic Ruling
Beyond the "Beit Yosef," Rabbi Shimshon's influence can be found in many halakhic works:
Keset ha-Sofer: the work of Rabbi Shlomo Ganzfried, which became the basic textbook for scribes in the 19th century, relies to a great extent on the rules laid down in "Baruch She'amar."[10]
Mishnah Berurah: in the commentary "Mishnat Soferim," the Chofetz Chaim quotes "Baruch She'amar" in almost every paragraph dealing with the form of the letters.[9]
The rulings of the Ari: although some of the followers of the Ari changed certain forms (such as the inverted tzadi), they too rely on the foundations Rabbi Shimshon laid in clarifying the basic laws of processing the parchment and of writing.[5]
The Modern Importance of "Baruch She'amar"
In the modern era, in which the craft of STaM has become a large-scale industry, the book "Baruch She'amar" serves as a brake against decline to a merely technical level.[10, 11] It reminds the modern scribe that he is not merely a graphic artist but a link in a chain of transmission that reaches back to Sinai.[5] Collections of works on STaM published today still include the works of Rabbi Shimshon as an inseparable part of the core of required knowledge.[11]
Summary: The Figure of the Quiet Revolutionary of Prague
Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer "Baruch She'amar" represents the figure of a Torah scholar who succeeded in leaving an indelible imprint on the physiognomy of Jewish holiness.[1, 3] Through a Sisyphean effort of wandering, correcting and writing, he saved the form of the Hebrew letters from corruption and oblivion.[1, 2] A small orphan who became a supreme halakhic authority, Rabbi Shimshon proved that devotion in prayer (as his name attests) can become an engine for a wide-ranging repair of the world.[1, 2]
Every time a Jew opens a Torah scroll, puts on tefillin or kisses a mezuzah, he encounters the fruit of Rabbi Shimshon's labor.[4, 5] The letters gazing out from the parchment are the letters that he protected, whose form he made precise and whose secret he preserved.[1, 5] "Baruch She'amar" is not merely the name of a prayer or of a book; it is a symbol of an uncompromising Jewish commitment to transmitting the tradition with precision of every line and thorn, from generation to generation, forever.[1]

The teaching of Rabbi Shimshon Baruch She'amar is characterized by a meticulous approach resting on three legs: the tradition of the sages of Ashkenaz, research into the sources of the Geonim, and practical experience in the field. He saw the halakhic text not merely as theoretical instruction but as manufacturer's instructions that must be carried out with almost mathematical precision in order to ensure the holiness of the object.[1, 2, 3]
The Use of Ancient Sources
Rabbi Shimshon was greatly versed in the writings of the Geonim and the early Rishonim. In his glosses he constantly quotes the "Halakhot Gedolot" and the "Shimusha Rabba," an ancient work on the laws of tefillin attributed to the Geonim.[2, 8] He dealt extensively with the description of the "square knot" of the tefillin, relying on ancient versions of Rav Hai Gaon and of Rabbi Yehuda ben Barzilai of Barcelona.[8] His ability to draw information from forgotten sources and make it accessible to scribes turned his book into a kind of encyclopedia of the craft of STaM.
The Struggle over the Form of the Letters and the "Beit Yosef Script"
One of Rabbi Shimshon's most central contributions is the shaping of what is called today the "Beit Yosef script."[4, 5] Although it was Rabbi Yosef Karo who published the laws in section 36 of Orach Chaim, he himself declares that he relies on the book "Baruch She'amar" in all that concerns the custom of Ashkenaz and the form of their letters.[4, 5] Rabbi Shimshon defined with great precision the relations between the parts of the letter, the placement of the crownlets (Tagin), and the laws concerning the "thorn of the yod" according to the view of Rabbenu Tam.[5]
Rabbi Shimshon's precision touched the smallest details:
Sha'atnez Getz (shin, ayin, tet, nun, zayin, gimel, tzadi): insistence on three crownlets above these letters.[5]
Bedek Chayah (bet, dalet, kuf, chet, yod, he): insistence on one crownlet above these letters.[5]
Melakhet Sofer (mem, lamed, alef, kaf, tav, samekh, vav, peh, resh): letters without crownlets, but with specific design requirements.[5]
The Controversy over the "Inverted Tzadi": Between Tradition and Kabbalah
A fascinating question that demonstrates Rabbi Shimshon's lasting influence is the debate over the form of the letter tzadi.[9] According to the description appearing in "Baruch She'amar," the letter tzadi is composed of a bent nun with a yod on it whose head faces right (a straight form). This is the classical Ashkenazi tradition that Rabbi Shimshon perpetuated.[9]
With the spread of the Kabbalah and the writings of the Ari, a custom developed of writing the yod on the back of the tzadi "inverted," that is, facing left. This controversy accompanied the world of STaM for hundreds of years.[9] Whereas the Sephardic tradition and some of the Hasidim adopted the "inverted tzadi," the decisors loyal to the tradition of "Baruch She'amar," headed in recent generations by the "Chazon Ish," insisted that the ancient Ashkenazi tradition brought in the book must not be changed.[9] This debate illustrates how a book written in the 14th century continues to be a firm rock for halakhic discussion in the 20th and 21st centuries as well.
The History of the Printing and Preservation of "Baruch She'amar"
For hundreds of years the book "Baruch She'amar" circulated in manuscripts only.[7] Scribes used to copy it for themselves as part of their professional training. An 18th-century manuscript found recently attests to the level of precision with which the work was preserved, with a clear separation between the original text of Rabbi Avraham and the glosses of Rabbi Shimshon.[7]
The transition to print was not free of difficulties:
The Shklov edition (1804): regarded as one of the central editions, but it suffers from editing and printing corruptions.[2, 3] This edition also included the "Otiyot de-Rabbi Akiva" and further kabbalistic passages that had been added to the book over time.[2, 3]
The Warsaw edition (1877): the Reizman edition, which provided a more accessible text and served students of STaM in Europe at the end of the 19th century.[4]
The fact that the book was printed again and again in the Torah centers of eastern Europe attests that it never lost its importance as a foundational book.[4, 7]
Influence on Later Generations and Its Place in the Jewish Bookcase
The legacy of Rabbi Shimshon Baruch She'amar is not confined to the bookshelf of the scribes of STaM. It forms a bridge between the period of the Rishonim and the period of the Acharonim and a source of authority for everyone who deals with the laws of writing and holiness.

Beyond the "Beit Yosef," Rabbi Shimshon's influence can be found in many halakhic works:

The rulings of the Ari: although some of the followers of the Ari changed certain forms (such as the inverted tzadi), they too rely on the foundations Rabbi Shimshon laid in clarifying the basic laws of processing the parchment and of writing.[5]
The Modern Importance of "Baruch She'amar"
In the modern era, in which the craft of STaM has become a large-scale industry, the book "Baruch She'amar" serves as a brake against decline to a merely technical level.[10, 11] It reminds the modern scribe that he is not merely a graphic artist but a link in a chain of transmission that reaches back to Sinai.[5] Collections of works on STaM published today still include the works of Rabbi Shimshon as an inseparable part of the core of required knowledge.[11]
Summary: The Figure of the Quiet Revolutionary of Prague
Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer "Baruch She'amar" represents the figure of a Torah scholar who succeeded in leaving an indelible imprint on the physiognomy of Jewish holiness.[1, 3] Through a Sisyphean effort of wandering, correcting and writing, he saved the form of the Hebrew letters from corruption and oblivion.[1, 2] A small orphan who became a supreme halakhic authority, Rabbi Shimshon proved that devotion in prayer (as his name attests) can become an engine for a wide-ranging repair of the world.[1, 2]

The Halakhic Teaching and Public Work of Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer (Baruch She'amar): A Renaissance of the Craft of STaM in Ashkenaz and the Land of Israel
The article surveys the monumental work of Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer, called "Baruch She'amar," who worked in the 14th century to restore and establish the craft of STaM (Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot) in Ashkenaz and the Land of Israel. The text describes how a young orphan became a supreme halakhic authority whose canonical work, the book "Baruch She'amar," constitutes to this day the main foundation for the laws of writing the letters and their form, known as the **"Beit Yosef script"**. The source emphasizes Rabbi Shimshon's journeys to correct corruptions in the scribal tradition and the unique literary structure of his work, which combines halakha, technical tradition and kabbalistic secrets. Ultimately, the article presents his figure as a historical bridge that ensured the continuity of the sacred tradition and of halakhic precision from generation to generation.
The Halakhic Teaching and Public Work of Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer (Baruch She'amar): A Renaissance of the Craft of STaM in Ashkenaz and the Land of Israel
Historical Introduction: The World of STaM in the Fourteenth Century
The history of the writing of Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot (STaM) underwent significant changes during the fourteenth century, a period in which the Ashkenazi traditions of halakhic ruling took shape in the face of the challenges of the time and of wandering. At the center of this process stands the figure of Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer, called "Baruch She'amar," whose work went beyond mere halakhic instruction and became an enterprise of rescuing ancient scribal traditions and establishing them for later generations.[1, 2] The fourteenth century was characterized by instability for the communities of Ashkenaz, which at times led to neglect of the complex sacred crafts and to the penetration of corruptions into the form of the letters and into the laws of making tefillin.[1, 2] Rabbi Shimshon, who lived and worked in Germany, Prague and the Land of Israel, identified this neglect and devoted his life to remedying the situation, combining deep scholarly knowledge of halakha with supreme technical skill in the scribal craft.[2, 3]
Rabbi Shimshon's importance derives not only from his personality but mainly from the canonical work he left behind – the book "Baruch She'amar." This book is not a single unit but a fabric of knowledge combining the teaching of great Rishonim, among them Rabbi Avraham of Sinzheim (a disciple of the Maharam of Rothenburg), with the glosses and insights of Rabbi Shimshon himself, to which was later added the "Alpha Beta" of his disciple, Rabbi Yom Tov Lipmann Mühlhausen.[1, 4] The influence of this work is so profound that most of the laws of STaM appearing in the "Shulchan Arukh" and known as the "Beit Yosef script" derive directly from the traditions Rabbi Shimshon perpetuated in his writings.[4, 5]
A Biography of Devotion: From Orphanhood to Leadership
Rabbi Shimshon ben Eliezer was born in the land of Saxony (Sachsen) in Germany at the beginning of the 14th century.[1, 2] In his childhood he moved with his parents to the city of Prague, which was at that time a central Torah crossroads in Europe. When he was only about eight years old, the young Shimshon experienced a severe personal tragedy when he was orphaned of both his parents.[1, 2, 3] This orphanhood did not break his spirit, but led him to find refuge and meaning within the walls of the synagogue and in the care of the sages of the generation.
The Origin of the Name "Baruch She'amar" and Its Family Consequences
The epithet "Baruch She'amar," which accompanied Rabbi Shimshon and over the years became his family name, grew out of a distinctive religious practice he adopted in his childhood.[1, 3] In the introduction to his book he relates that he used to rise early for the synagogue and recite the prayer "Baruch She'amar" ("Blessed is He who spoke") in the pleasant and sweet voice with which the blessed Lord had graced him.[1] The devotion and joy with which he recited the prayer impressed the congregation, until they called him "Shimshon Baruch She'amar."[1, 2, 3] This name did not remain merely a personal epithet; according to the testimony of the Chida in his book "Shem ha-Gedolim," the name became a family inheritance passed down from generation to generation, and references can be found in the "Beit Yosef" to Rabbi Yitzhak Baruch She'amar, who was apparently one of his descendants.[2, 3, 4]
Professional Apprenticeship under Rabbi Yissachar
After he was orphaned, Rabbi Shimshon was adopted by Rabbi Yissachar, who was an expert scribe and a Torah scholar.[2, 3] Rabbi Yissachar recognized the potential latent in the boy and taught him the craft of writing tefillin, mezuzot and Torah scrolls.[2] This apprenticeship was critical, for it not only gave Shimshon a profession but brought him into the chain of transmission of the Ashkenazi scribal craft, which demands precision in technical and halakhic details alike.[2, 3]
Wandering as a Mission of Correction: From Europe to Jerusalem
Rabbi Shimshon did not content himself with staying in one place. He set out on an extensive journey throughout central and eastern Europe, which included Austria, Poland, Lusatia, Thuringia and Bavaria.[2, 3] In every community he came to, he acted as an inspector and instructor for the local scribes of STaM. He discovered great neglect; many scribes did not know the precise halakha, and grave errors had become entrenched in the writing of the letters and in the processing of the parchment.[1, 2] In certain cases his halakhic position was so firm that he instructed certain scribes to stop writing altogether, out of concern that the public would be misled and that invalid sacred objects would come from their hands.[1]
The Encounter with the Scribes of the Land of Israel and the Halakhic Disappointment
The high point of his journeys was his ascent to the Land of Israel.[1, 2] Rabbi Shimshon came to the Land expecting to find there the pure source of the sacred craft, on the assumption that the scribes of the Land preserved the tradition most precisely.[2, 3] However, his hope was disappointed. On arriving in Jerusalem and in other communities in the Land, he discovered that most of the scribes there suffered from deep ignorance regarding the accepted halakha and the traditional form of the letters.[2, 3, 6] This discovery was the main motive for writing his work, since he understood that the need for "correction" was not limited to Ashkenaz alone but was an urgent need of all Jewry. He used his findings in the Land of Israel to establish the need for an orderly halakhic work that would serve as a binding guide for every scribe wherever he might be.[2, 3]

The book "Baruch She'amar" as we know it today is in fact a collection bringing together three separate works that merged over the generations into a single halakhic entity.[1, 4] Understanding this structure is essential for assessing the contribution of Rabbi Shimshon, who acted not only as an author but also as an editor and corrector who preserved ancient texts.
